Can Trump really win?

The answer most certainly is yes.

On polling average over the last seven days, Trump’s vote has increased, his position in a number of swing states has improved and the polling trend is running his way not Clinton’s.

A number of forecasts continue to show Trump as having a one in ten chance of winning the election but the most reliable forecaster, Nate Silver at fivethirtyeight.com puts Trump’s chance at a touch under one in six.

The bookies (the miserable swine) are never going to go broke offering Trump at 4/1 but that is where he stands in the betting markets with Clinton at $1.15.

Trump won’t win the popular vote but that really is only a popularity contest. The only thing that matters is getting to 270 electoral college votes. Trump’s pathways to 270 are limited but one scenario requires Trump to carry Florida, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Arizona.

On polling average Clinton leads Florida by less than 2 points, less than 3 in North Carolina, Pennsylvania by 5 and less than a point in Arizona. Trump holds a narrow lead in Ohio. With the exception of Pennsylvania, the margin is within a standard polling margin of error of around three points. In this scenario I have presumed Trump wins Iowa where he currently holds a narrow lead over Clinton.

Clearly, everything would have to go right for the man with the spider monkey hair extension but it is not beyond the realms of possibility.

But if Pennsylvania stays blue, can Trump pick up the 20 electoral college votes elsewhere? That would require an unlikely win in a state like New Mexico where Clinton leads by 8, a win in Nevada where he trails by a couple of points and Utah where Trump leads over the third party candidate, Evan McMullin. Clinton can’t win in Utah but if McMullin gets up, that would amount to Trump having to find another six college votes from a state like Colorado where he trails by 6.

If it all sounds terribly complex and relies on far too many assumptions, the best way to approach the presidential election as a spectator sport is the knowledge that most of the action will take place in the first quarter. By early afternoon on Wednesday November 9 AEDT, the results of the eastern states will be through and the winner should be known or at least we’ll know that it’s going to be a nail biter.

If Trump loses Florida it’s all over. But even if he does buck the polling in the Sunshine State, he can’t afford to lose North Carolina. However, if he carries them both a narrow Trump win becomes a real possibility.
